Pictured here working from his bed on January 28th 1967, not long before he sadly passed away.

Stephen Joseph (1921–1967) was a visionary British theatre pioneer who founded the UK's first professional theatre-in-the-round company.

Joseph served as the principal mentor and teacher to a young Alan Ayckbourn, employing him as an actor and challenging him to write his very own plays. Ayckbourn eventually took over Joseph’s Scarborough company, cementing its reputation for world premieres.

Alan Ayckbourn's classic 1971 play Time & Time Again is touring this summer to Devonshire Park Theatre, Eastbourne, from 28 July to 1 August; the Lyceum Theatre, Crewe, from 5 - 8 August; the Wyvern Theatre, Swinburn, from 20 - 22 August.

The play is being produced by Phil & Ben Productions, which has previously produced several Ayckbourn plays for tour. 

The production will star Pete Ashmore as Leonard, Katy Dean as Anna, Phil Stewart as Graham, Simon Pothecary as Peter and Tanya-Loretta Dee as Joan, who has appeared in several Ayckbourn world premieres directed by the playwright.

The play centres on Leonard, an ambivalent teacher who lives with his sister Anna and husband Graham. When he is introduced to the sports-mad Peter and his attractive fiancee, Joan, all their lives are changed. As Leonard tries to win the affection of Joan, Peter tries to engage him in the local sports scene for which he is terminally unsuited whilst Graham looks on jealously.

A new edition of Simon Murgatroyd's book A Theatrical Revolution has been published to tie in with The Library Theatre at 70 exhibition, which is running at Scarborough Library until 27 June.

A Theatrical Revolution explores the inaugural year of The Library Theatre in 1955 and how it was created by Stephen Joseph alongside the challenges it faced.

It includes an exclusive preface and interview with Sir Alan Ayckbourn CBE, an in-depth look at the creation and first year of the company, contemporary articles by Stephen Joseph, a timeline of the Library Theatre as well as rarely seen photographs from the first year.

A Theatrical Revolution is written by Alan Ayckbourn's archivist and theatre historian Simon Murgatroyd and is priced at £10 (including P&P, UK only) directly from Simon. It is also expected to be available from online bookstores in the next few weeks.

The 50th anniversary of the opening of the Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round is being celebrated in a talk with Alan Ayckbourn's archivist this June.

The Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round - colloquially known as Westwood - was the second home of theatre in the round in Scarborough from 1976 - 1996 (after The Library Theatre and before the Stephen Joseph Theatre) and was where the company cemented its national and international reputation. It remains, to this day, Alan Ayckbourn's favourite of the three venues.

The theatre opened in October 1996 following a 60 day transformation (!) from school to theatre. Simon will be talking about why the company moved, how this took place and the legacy of this venue to both Scarborough and the wider theatre scene.

A Round 50 - Theatre in the Round at Westwood is taking place at Woodend Gallery and Studios on Saturday 20 June air 1pm. Tickets are £5 and available from www.scarboroughfair.uk/fringe/.

The event is part of the Scarborough fringe and the Scarborough 400 celebrations.

The Library Theatre at 70 exhibition is now running at Scarborough Library and features a number of people who would go on to fame.

The curator, Simon Murgatroyd M.A., has picked nine faces from the display. Can you name them? Answers below.

The Library Theatre at 70 exhibit has more than 90 photos celebrating the 21 years the UK's first professional theatre-in-the-round company spent at Scarborough Library. There's production images., behind-the-scenes images, companies and a celebration of Alan Ayckbourn's plays which premiered there.

The display is free and can be seen until 27 June on the first floor of Scarborough Library during normal Library opening hours.

The answers are - very concisely! – are 1) Tom Baker (1968) – most famous as the fourth regeneration of The Doctor in the long-running TV series Doctor Who; 2) John Nettles (1967) – the star of TV’s Bergerac and Midsomer Murders; 3) Stephanie Turner (1970) – actor and director who gained fame as the star of the BBC series Juliet Bravo; 4) Robert Powell (1967) – starred in in the BBC series Doomwatch soon after working in Scarborough, but found international fame in the titular role of Jesus of Nazareth; 5) Martin Carthy (1960) – then a stage manager at the Library Theatre, who became one of the most influential figures in English folk music, inspiring the likes of Bob Dylan and Paul Simon; 6) Bob Peck (1970) – BAFTA winning and Olivier nominated actor most famed for the BBC series Edge of Darkness and Jurassic Park; 7) Christopher Godwin – famed stage and screen actor currently appearing opposite Mark Gatiss in the RSC production of The Resistable Rise of Arturo Ui; 8) Malcom Hebden (1976) – actor most fondly known as Norris in the soap opera Coronation Street; 9) Alan Ayckbourn (1957) – quite a famous playwright…

The Library Theatre at 70 exhibition is now open at Scarborough Library and running until 27 June.

The photographic exhibition celebrates the launch of the UK's first professional theatre-in-the-round by Stephen Joseph on the first floor of Scarborough Library.

It features 90 photographs chronicling the plays, people and life of the company from 1955 to 1976, when the company moved to its second home. It is curated by Alan Ayckbourn's archivist and theatre historian, Simon Murgatroyd M.A.

For the 2026 exhibition, more than half the photographs are new for this year with many never previously shown in public. Also new for this year is a section dedicated to the Ayckbourn plays which premiered at the Library Theatre, many of which went onto West End and global success.

The Library Theatre at 70 exhibition is free and on the first floor of Scarborough Library during normal library opening hours until 27 June. Further details can be found at www.a-round-town.com

The website, A Round Town, which celebrates the early history of theatre in the round in Scarborough, has just had a huge overhaul with more than 500 pages added by theatre historian and Alan Ayckbourn's archivist, Simon Murgatroyd

There's now a page for every single production produced at both Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre (1955 - 1976) and the Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round (1976 - 1996) as well as for notable announced but unproduced plays. That's more 400 new pages.

The website has also added technical details about both venues - including floorpans and historic pricing structures - as well as expanding the pages relating to company and staff pages. That's all on top of the existing 1,500 pages about the venues, company and its history.

If you're interested in the UK's first professional theatre in the round, its people, plays and history or want to understand why this venue is so essential to Alan Ayckbourn's career or why Stephen Joseph should be regarded as an important figure in British theatre history then head to www.a-round-town.com

Standing Room Only (1961) is Alan Ayckbourn's fourth play and - in my opinion as his archivist - the first where his original playwriting voice is heard. 

It's also his first piece of speculative fiction (set in the distant, gridlocked dystopian future of... 2010), his first play to be optioned for both the West End and television (neither sadly produced) and the earliest play to be actually credited to him rather than his pseudonym of Roland Allen. 

It's also unavailable to read outside of the Borthwick Institute for Archives and the British Library. But you can find out more about this fascinating play in my latest deep-dive into Alan's plays at Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre on the Ayckbourn Blog...

Yesterday afternoon, Sir Alan Ayckbourn was presented with the ABTT (Association of British Theatre Technicians) Stephen Joseph Lifetime Achievement Award in recognition of his outstanding contribution to the development of Theatre in the Round in Britain.

It is the first time he has been recognised for this specific achievement and it was a very special moment to see him receive this award; the result of a lifetime championing theatre in the round and the legacy of Stephen Joseph.

It is inconceivable that without Alan and his dedication and drive, the legacy and work of Stephen Joseph would have even survived, let alone thrived in Scarborough. It was Alan who took up the reins of the company after Stephen's death and firmly embedded the founding principles and ambitions of this singular and inspirational man in the Scarborough company - new writing, theatre in the round and championing regional theatre.

Without Alan, there would undoubtedly be no Stephen Joseph Theatre today, no theatre in the round in Scarborough and the memory of what Stephen Joseph began and achieved in this town would, inarguably, have been lost to time. It is only right this achievement is recognised and so appropriately with an award bearing the name of the man who had been the most significant influence and inspiration in Alan's life.

Congratulation, Sir Alan, this recognition is long overdue and so very well deserved.

Pictured: Sir Alan receiving the Stephen Joseph Lifetime Achievement award from Liz Sillett, CEO of the ABTT (right) with Bob Millington, chair of the Stephen Joseph Committee who read the citation (left, standing on stage) at the Stephen Joseph Theatre on Sunday 28 September 2025.

The Library Theatre at 70 exhibition is almost here! It runs from Thursday 10 - Saturday 12 July on the first floor of Scarborough Library and is free.

On 14 July 1955, Stephen Joseph launched the UK’s first professional in-the-round company in Scarborough - predicated on championing theatre in the round and new writing.

The theatre pioneer was reacting against the established and predominant proscenium arch form and the way, he believed, it was suffocating British theatre and preventing it from exploring the potential of theatre and new work.

It was a hugely significant moment in British theatre and Stephen’s legacy would be carried on by his protégé Alan Ayckbourn, who also championed theatre in the round, new writing and new writers.

Between them, they were responsible for guiding theatre in the round in Scarborough through its first 55 years and that story is told and celebrated at www.a-round-town.com

Here the story of theatre in the round from 1955 to 2009 is told, emphasising its contribution to Scarborough’s cultural heritage and history whilst celebrating how Stephen Joseph and Alan Ayckbourn placed Scarborough on the theatrical map during the company’s pioneering first five decades.

One of the most frequent questions received by Alan Ayckbourn’s Official Website is whether an Ayckbourn play can be updated to the present day?

On the Ayckbourn Blog, the playwright’s archivist - Simon Murgatroyd - tackles the question to show why, essentially, the majority of Alan Ayckbourn’s works are period pieces.

That Alan is not a timeless writer, but a writer of his time and his plays are a social document of what it was to live in the UK between the 1960s and the 2020s.

That any attempt to update the plays or move them to a modern setting essentially misunderstands the play and the playwright and often leaves the plays making no sense.

A long thought lost 1977 radio adaptation of Alan Ayckbourn’s classic play Absurd Person Singular has been rediscovered.

First broadcast on Saturday Night Theatre on BBC Radio 4 1977, this adaptation of Absurd Person Singular has never been repeated and was presumed lost with next to no details known about it.

It has now been found in archive and will be broadcast on BBC Radio 4 Extra and BBC Sounds from 30 May 2024, having been unheard for more than 45 years.

One of the most significant facts about the play is it features Christopher Godwin playing the role of Sidney Hopcroft; Christopher appeared in the world premiere production of the play at Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre, Scarborough, in 1972 playing Ronald.

Considered one of Alan Ayckbourn’s most significant and funniest plays, the production stars Judy Parfitt as Marion, Stephen Murray as Ronald and Christopher Godwin as Sidney.

Today marks the 28th anniversary of the Stephen Joseph Theatre opening in its present home in Scarborough’s former Odeon cinema.

On 24 April 1996, the Stephen Joseph Theatre opened its doors for the first time with a production of Alan Ayckbourn and Andrew Lloyd Webber’s hit musical By Jeeves.

The venue had been more than five years in the making and was a £5.2m renovation of the 1936 built Odeon cinema converted into a state-of-the-art theatre with two auditoria.

The company has previously been based at the Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre (1955 - 1976) and the Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round (1976 - 1995).

Alan Ayckbourn was Artistic Director of the new venue from 1996 to 2009 and oversaw the transition to the company’s first permanent home, finally fulfilling the dream of Stephen Joseph for the company he founded to have a purpose-designed theatre in the round space.

Although Alan Ayckbourn stepped down as Artistic Director 15 years ago after almost four decades in that role, he still premieres new work at the venue.

Next up is his 90th play, Show & Tell, which opens at the theatre from 5 September to 5 October 2024. Full details can be found at the theatre’s website.

Book find of the day!

This was a pleasant surprise with the impulse buy of a previously unfamiliar work - Jack Mitchley and Peter Spalding’s 5,000 Years of Theatre (Batsford Ltd, 1982).

Mitchley is significant because in 1948, theatre pioneer - and Alan Ayckbourn’s mentor - Stephen Joseph experienced theatre in the round for the very first time when he saw Mitchley’s amateur company performing in Norfolk (at the time theatre in the round was, essentially, an unknown quantity in the UK).

Stephen Joseph wrote of the experience, “I enjoyed the performance immensely and returned to the repertory theatre with a bee beginning to buzz in the back of my mind.”

Over the next few years, Joseph would experience theatre in the round in America before setting up, in 1955, the UK’s first professional theatre in the round company at Scarborough Library. There, two years later, Alan Ayckbourn joined the company as an actor.

What is nice about the book discovery is it comes full circle as the final pages see Mitcheey talking about theatre in the round and adaptable theatres, making specific reference to Stephen and his theatre in the round ventures in Scarborough and Stoke-on-Trent, which were inspired by Stephen’s first encounter of the form with Mitchley.

You can find out more about the history of theatre in the round in Scarborough and Stephen Joseph at www.a-round-town.com

Westwood - as it was colloquially known - was the second home of theatre in the round in Scarborough.

Alan Ayckbourn moved to what was presumed to be a temporary home at the old Municipal School beneath Valley Bridge in 1976, where it opened as Theatre in the Round at Westwood.

Two years later - and with it obvious it was to become a more permanent home to the company - it was renamed the Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round.

It is probably Alan Ayckbourn’s favourite of the three homes of theatre in the round in the town and would be where the company gained national and international recognition.

Over the course of 20 years, it produced 233 plays of which 106 were world premieres by the likes of Tim Firth, Vanessa Brooks, Stephen Mallatratt, Peter Tinniswood, Alison Skilbeck and, of course, Alan Ayckbourn.

You can find out in-depth details about the venue, the people who worked there, its history and the plays produced at Westwood at www.a-round-town.com which looks at the history of theatre in the round in Scarborough between 1955 and 2009. It is curated by Alan Ayckbourn’s archivist & theatre historian Simon Murgatroyd M.A.

One of Alan Ayckbourn’s most successful plays is Relatively Speaking, premiered in 1965 at Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre, Scarborough, before catapulting Alan to success in the West End in 1967.

It’s an acclaimed play but it does have one puzzling issue. Why did Alan Ayckbourn write such a monumental change of scenes between the first and second scene? The transition from a fully realised flat to a garden and patio would seem to be best suited to an interval transition not a quick change of action.

So why did Alan do it? The answer had been forgotten by the playwright, but we now know why he did it and how it was achieved in the original production. And how nothing that followed remotely reflected what Alan originally had in mind.

The answer’s in the photo taken from the original production - hidden in plain sight!

You can find out the full story and the answer on the Ayckbourn blog at http://blog.alanayckbourn.net or via the bio link.

Our final entry of 2023 for the complete guide to Alan Ayckbourn’s plays brings us to the end of 1982 and Alan’s first adaptation of an existing play, A Trip To Scarborough.

Very loosely adapted from R.B. Sheridan’s original, it maintains the barest of plots from the Restoration drama and adds and interweaves two plot lines from the early 1940s and the present day.

As such it charts the decline of the hero from swashbuckling fop to untrustworthy con artist as well as knocking the ‘superiority’ of the Metropolitan to the regional.

It was a huge success in Scarborough when it premiered on 8 December 1982 at the Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round with an excellent cast which included John Arthur, Russell Dixon, Michael Cashman and Elizabeth Kelly.

Revivals have been rare, most notably at the New Vic, Newcastle-under-Lyme, in 1987 and at the Stephen Joseph Theatre in 2007. It remains the only Ayckbourn work to be specifically set in his home town of Scarborough. 

This post is dedicated to the memory of Russell Dixon who died earlier this year. Russell was a consummate Ayckbourn actor who was a joy to know. He will be sadly missed.

One of the highlights of the Ayckbourn Collection at Scarborough Museums and Galleries is a piece that brings the ground-breaking playwright Harold Pinter into the theatre in the round story.

Alan Ayckbourn is well known for introducing water elements into his work - you need only think of the canal for Way Upstream or the swimming pool in Man of the Moment.

They all trace back to 1971 and Alan’s first use of a water feature in one of his works with a garden pond in Time & Time Again - which can be seen on the left of this photo.

It was a feature not easily forgotten, not least by Scarborough library where the production premiered at Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre in the Concert Room on the first floor. One night, post-show, the pond developed a leak and began to drip, drip, drip…

The next morning the library staff found the water had leaked into the reading room beneath, apparently affecting the periodicals. The library was reported to be distinctly unamused and Alan didn’t introduce another water feature in his work until the company moved homes in 1976.

Which would lead to Way Upstream in 1981. But that’s another story…

‘Theatre In The Round’ is the most important work Stephen Joseph wrote during his lifetime. It is one four books written by the theatre pioneer, but this is his most personal and draws upon a decade of experience.

It offers his view of theatre in the round - then a largely unknown and unexplored form of staging in contemporary British theatre - and approaches it from a technical, practical and philosophical stance, arguing its merits and advantages.

Two of the chapters also look at the history of the first decade of Theatre on the Round at the Library Theatre, Scarborough - home to the UK’s first professional theatre in the round company.

‘Theatre In The Round’ its an essential book for anyone interested in Stephen Joseph, the development of theatre in the round historically as well as in Scarborough or just interested in the practicalities of theatre in the round.

The book was published in 1967, the year of Stephen Joseph’s death. It is, sadly, out of print but can occasionally be found via second-hand booksellers. A copy is currently on display in The Ayckbourn Collection.

This was a collaboration with the composer Paul Todd and is set in a recording studio - apparently inspired by some of Alan’s experiences as a BBC Radio Drama Producer between 1965 and 1970.

Joseph, of course, founded Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre in Scarborough in 1955. He was a theatre pioneer who became a mentor to Alan Ayckbourn and commissioned him to both first write and direct.

He was also a prolific artist - be it sketches such as this or architectural designs for theatre in the round spaces - and he illustrated the majority of his books on theatre.

There are two Joseph drawings in the Ayckbourn Collection, both on display currently at Scarborough Art Gallery, and this one is fascinating as it shows a circular theatre in the round. Stephen never realised any of his ideas for a circular / oblong space during his life, but in 1986 - 19 years after his death - the company he founded in Stoke on Trent in 1962 moved from the Victoria Theatre to the New Vic in Newcastle-under-Lyme.

There the former rectangular staging was replaced by a circular space with a gallery - much as Stephen had illustrated here.

Of all Alan Ayckbourn and Paul Todd’s musical revues, Me, Myself and I is probably the most well-known and successful.

It premiered at the Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round, Scarborough, on 2 June 1981 - initially in three parts over three performances: ‘Me’, ‘Myself’ and ‘I’ - directed by Alan Ayckbourn with the resident company and musicians.

The individual parts were later condensed into a single revue which premiered at the Orange Tree, Richmond, in 1982, directed by Kim Grant - where it was also revived in 1983 and 2003.

Alan Ayckbourn also directed it at the National Theatre in 1985 in the Lyttelton Buffet, whilst he was at the National directing A Chorus of Disapproval.

The revue looks at the life of a young mum of four, recently voted ‘mum of the year’, whose life is complicated by the fact that two other sides of her personality (Myself and I) interrupt the narrative and none of the three personalities can agree on much.

It is the only revue of Alan Ayckbourn and Paul Todd’s to have been published by Samuel French.

Practically since Stephen Joseph opened Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre in Scarborough in 1955, there were attempts to find a permanent home for the company. All met with no success - until 1996!

One of the most promising proposals came in 1970 with a theatre-in-the-round with restaurant being built in The Crescent / Valley Gardens creating a cultural quarter for the town next to the Art Gallery and, then, Natural History Museum.

The plan was vetoed by the council and strongly opposed by residents in The Crescent - including the theatre’s own chairman, Tom Laughton, who resigned from the theatre board.

The proposed site - still undeveloped today - can still be seen in The Crescent today.

All aboard for this week’s entry in the complete guide to Alan Ayckbourn’s writing with his 27th full-length play Way Upstream.

Premiered on 2 October 1981 at the Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round, Scarborough, this extraordinary work is set on a river cruiser on water. Real water. The stage is flooded to give the illusion of a boat travelling up the river orb. And there’s a real rain-storm too. Front rows tend to get a bit wet during productions of this play.

A huge hit in Scarborough on its premiere and subsequent revival in 2003. The play gained notoriety when it temporarily closed the National Theatre in 1982 after the water tank burst and spilt tens of thousands of gallons of water into the bowels of the NT.

Despite this, the play actually did well at the NT and - with a number of strong revivals over the decades - has come to be reappraised as one of the playwright’s key works of the 1980s. It’s certainly - technically - one of his most ambitious!

It was also adapted as a film by The BBC in 1988 and for the radio in 1997. Although the only way to truly appreciate this play is when you step into a familiar theatre and see the stage covered by a small ‘lake’ of water. A truly magical theatrical experience!

Within the current display is a poster and programme for one of Alan Ayckbourn’s most popular works, Confusions. They might perhaps be considered odd pieces compared to highlight compared to some of the more obvious rarities on display.

But the poster is probably unique - the only known surviving poster for the world premiere premiere of Confusions at Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre, Scarborough, in 1974 and the programme one of the rarest for one of his popular works.

They are also historically significant in that Confusions marked the point when Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre essentially became a year round concern. Having been operating on summer only seasons between 1962 and 1973, in 1974 Alan used Confusions to launch both a winter and touring season for the company.

So, aside from the fact it’s a rather nice design, the poster is both an Ayckbourn rarity and a mark of a significant shift in the history of theatre in the round in Scarborough.

1967
In 1967, Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre in Scarborough resumed professional productions after its founder, Stephen Joseph, had closed the company in 1965.

Despite the 18 month break, it would go from strength-to-strength over the subsequent decades and become a permanent and significant feature of Scarborough’s cultural heritage.

But 1967 was also notable for the death of the company’s founder, Stephen Joseph. At just 46 years old, Stephen died in Scarborough from cancer, diagnosed the previous year.

Stephen was a pioneer and extraordinary force in British theatre - even if his achievements are largely unrecognised today. He founded the UK’s first professional theatre in the round company and venue as well as the UK’s first drama department at the University of Manchester. He was a founding member of the Association of British Theatre Technicians and the Society of Theatre Consultants and he wrote several books promoting ‘new’ theatre forms. He championed new plays and new writers.

But more than that, he was an inspiration. He inspired those he worked with, those he taught and those he met. Many people would go on to become significant figures in British theatre as a result of their time with Stephen - not least Alan Ayckbourn, who credits him as being the most influential person of his entire life and career.

He died far too young and who knows what he might have achieved had he lived longer. But as Alan Ayckbourn once said, Stephen was the rocket that boosted so many of the people who admired him and his ideas to the stars.

It’s quarter of a century as we reach the 25th of Alan Ayckbourn’s full-lengths plays in the complete guide to his works.

Suburban Strains premiered at the Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round, Scarborough, on 18 January 1980 and was the first time Alan had attempted to write a musical since Jeeves (1975). It marked the first full-length musical collaboration between Alan and the composer Paul Todd.

The ambitious piece - described by Alan as a play with music - involved the installation of a double revolve in the Scarborough venue to indicate the movement back or forwards of time.

So successful was Suburban Strains, it was revived the following year in Scarborough; this production then transferred in its entirety to The Round House, London, in 1981 in an abortive attempt by Alan to circumvent the West End, which he had increasingly become frustrated with.

The London production did not do well critically nor commercially and the piece has rarely been produced professionally since.

Of note, it is the first full-length play at the Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round to have its own original cast recording, which was recorded in-house and released on audio cassette.

1966
It’s not widely known that at the end of the summer of the 1965 summer season, Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre, Scarborough, was closed by its founder - Stephen Joseph. Financial pressures, a perceived lack of support and failure by the Town Council and Library Committee to address previously raised issues led Stephen to announce the company’s tenure in Scarborough was over.

But theatre manager Ken Boden had other ideas and - with the support of the British Drama League and other key figures from the company’s history - managed to arrange an amateur season for the summer of 1966,

Very little Is known about the season other than its  schedule (pictured) and the fact Ken was also able to continue the annual Theatre in the Round festival. A rep season of four plays over eight weeks was arranged featuring local amateur companies Create Players, Filey Drama Club, Phoenix Drama Club and Outsiders Drama Club.

Behind the scenes, Ken worked tirelessly to find support and funding to revive the company as a professional operation for 1967. Although his and others’ endeavours would be successful, it was tinged with sadness as Stephen was aware by 1966 he had terminal cancer and would have little involvement in the company going forward.

Alan Ayckbourn is frequently described as a farceur, which is slightly odd given that of his 89 plays, the playwright considers only one of them is actually a farce…

That, of course, is Taking Steps, the playwright’s 24th full-length play, which premiered on 28 September 1979 at the Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round, Scarborough.

It was written specifically for performance in-the-round with three floors of a house overlaid on top of each other so action on different levels can happen simultaneously in one space. As the playwright noted, farce is quite difficult in the round so he replaced doors with floors.

It was the first play to have over 100 performances with its original Scarborough company and was revived in 1980, 1990 and 2017 in Scarborough to enormous success.

Less successful was its initial West End production which - despite Alan’s urging - was produced in the proscenium arch to no discernible advantage. Indeed the playwright has often noted there is no practical way to make the play work as intended when not produced in-the-round.

The complete guide to Alan Ayckbourn’s plays continues with Sisterly Feelings, his 23rd full-length play and the first to feature random elements. 

It premiered on 10 January 1979 at the Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round, Scarborough, and was unlike anything the playwright had attempted before.

There were alternative Act 1,ii and Act 2,i scenes which could be randomly decided on stage. The first with the flip of a coin. Famously, on the first night, the coin landed on its edge and rolled off stage!

It was the first of several ‘random’ plays including Mr A’s Amazing Maze Plays and Roundelay. It also notably removed a seating block in the original production to create a hill which could be free-wheeled down on a cycle.

The play later opened at the National Theatre on 3 and 4 June 1980 with Alan Ayckbourn and Christopher Morahan directing. Due to its scale and the random elements, it is rarely revived.

This has to be one of the most obscure produced Ayckbourn works ever…

In 1977 to mark the Silver Jubilee, Theatre in the Round at Westwood in Scarborough gave a one-off performance of a revue called The Jubilee Show with Alan collaborating with Mervyn Watson to produce a show which took a slightly surreal musical tour through the previous 25 years.

The entire company was involved alongside the pianist Michael Garrick and the amount of people on stage apparently outnumbered those in the audience…

This was due to late scheduling, lack of publicity and - in all likelihood - the fact the theatre had already had success that season with another celebratory show called Westwood Coronation Day Street Party.

Next to nothing survives about The Jubilee Show. It was never listed in brochures and subsequently omitted from official production lists. The playwright forgot all about it until 2007 when his archivist, Simon Murgatroyd, discovered the sole surviving manuscript stuffed at the back of a filing cabinet.

Its dubious place in the Ayckbourn canon was restored as a ‘Grey Play’ (produced once but never published nor available to produce) and the single manuscript is held in the Ayckbourn Archive at the Borthwick Institute for Archives at the University of York.

We’ve hit a new era in the complete guide to the works of Alan Ayckbourn with the move to the Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round in 1976.

This was the theatre in the round company’s second home in Scarborough and which they stayed until 1996.

The theatre was opened with a revival of Alan’s play Mr Whatnot - never previously performed in Scarborough - but Alan’s first new work for the new venue was Ten Times Table, which opened on 18 January 1977.

The play - which had the largest cast for an Ayckbourn play yet - was inspired by Alan’s experiences with all the committees he had encountered whilst trying to move the company to its new home. It was a big early hit for the company.

It then opened in The Globe Theatre (now The Gielgud) in London on 5 April 1978 and was the first Ayckbourn London production in the West End (rather than the National Theatre) to be directed by Alan and saw Christopher Godwin transfer from Scarborough to London repairing his role of Tim.

It’s a rare play from the period in never having been adapted for TV or radio, but in recent years it has seen a resurgence in popularity - possibly reflecting the divided politics of our times!

Here’s a question for Ayckbourn fans. What genre of play is Bedroom Farce?

0 Marks for anyone who says it’s a farce (it’s not), 1 point for a comedy (it is) and 2 points for it’s a play (Alan Ayckbourn prefers that term for the vast majority of his work).

In this complete guide to Alan Ayckbourn’s plays, Bedroom Farce is his 19th full-length play and premiered at Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre, Scarborough, on 16 June 1975.

It was actually commissioned though by the National Theatre as Alan’s first work for the NT, but as with all but one of his plays for the NT, it premiered in Scarborough first.

Interesting fact, it was commissioned by the NT as an end-stage work for the Lyttleton theatre but Alan intended to premiere it in-the-round in Scarborough, however a mis-measurement led to it being premiered three-sided instead… Confused yet?

It opened in the National Theatre on 16 Match 1977 and is regarded as the first bona fide hit of the NT in its South Bank home. It transferred into the West End 6 November 1978 and has the second longest run of any Ayckbourn production in London.

In 1979, the NT production opened on Broadway and in 1980, the production was also adapted for television by Granada TV with much of the original NT cast.

It has subsequently become one of the most popular and successful of Alan Ayckbourn’s plays.

We’ve now arrived at the first Ayckbourn musical in the guide to the complete plays.

In 1975, Alan Ayckbourn teamed up with the composer Andrew Lloyd Webber to write the musical Jeeves, based upon the works of P.G. Wodehouse.

Alan has no previous experience writing lyrics or the book for musicals. But that was OK. After all, even if the lyricist had never written lyrics, the composer had never composed for a ‘book’ musical and the director had never directed a musical.

On top of that, the designer and choreographer had both never worked on musicals before and the producer was completely absent.

What could possibly go wrong? As Alan once succinctly wrote “None of us knew what we were doing.”

Jeeves opened at Her Majesty’s Theatre, London, on 22 April 1975 and closed on 24 May 1975. It is one of the West End’s most notorious flops.

Still, in 1996 it was rewritten and revised as the award-winning By Jeeves by which point everyone concerned had a lot more experience and knew what they were doing. That did quite well, opening the SJT, transferring to the West End and then touring the UK and had been revived multiple times around the world. So it all came right in the end. Eventually.

Russell was one of the most prolific actors to have worked with Alan Ayckbourn in Scarborough over the years and appeared in the world premieres of 10 of his plays, as well as the premieres of several of Alan’s revues and adaptations and he also performed in a number of revivals.

Of all the plays he has written, Absent Friends is one of Alan Ayckbourn’s favourites.

Premiered at Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre, Scarborough, on 17 June 1974, it is also the first of his plays to take place in real time - time elapsed is the same for both characters and audience; in this case an excruciating two hour tea party!

We’re heading back into obscure Ayckbourn territory with the complete Ayckbourn play guide.

Can you guess how many produced screenplays Alan Ayckbourn has written? The answer: Just one. He’s been asked many times, but the playwright has only written one original screenplay for TV back in 1974.

This was ‘Service Not Included’ and it was commissioned by the BBC for its Masquerade drama series. Directed by Herbert Wise. It was broadcast on 20 May 1974 and has never been repeated. It ranks as one of the most obscure and little known produced Ayckbourn works.

It takes a waiter’s eye-view of an end of conference party at a hotel. Alan would re-use the narrative device later in the same year in the ‘Between Mouthfuls’ play in Confusions.

A copy of the original screenplay is held in the Ayckbourn Archive at the Borthwick Institute for Archives at the University of York, but other than that, a shooting schedule and a lone photo, nothing else is held in archive about this piece of Ayckbourn history.

We’re slightly out of order with the complete guide to Alan Ayckbourn’s plays because of The Norman Conquests last week.

We’re now going back a year to the play which preceded the trilogy, Absurd Person Singular, which premiered at Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre on 26 June 1972, directed by Alan Ayckbourn.

Alan won his first major award from this play - the Evening Standard Award for Best Comedy and it is one of the most revived and popular of his works.

Last year - on its 50th anniversary - the original lost manuscript for the play, very different to the final play, was discovered as well as the manuscript performed on the first night and subsequently cut by half-an-hour. The Story So Far… No, not a round-up of where we’re at in the complete guide to Alan Ayckbourn’s plays, but the name of his tenth play.

Although if you’re an Ayckbourn fan, you’d know it better as Family Circles - the fourth title it was given over the years!

The Story So Far… premiered at Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre on 20 August 1970. The cast included Bob Peck, Stephanie Turner and Elisabeth Sladen.

The following year, it went on a pre-West End tour titled Me Times Me Times Me which never got into the West End. The year after that, it went on another pre-West End tour with the title Me Times Me, which… never got into the West End.

In 1978, it finally received its London premiere, now called Family Circles, at the Orange Tree Theatre in Richmond.

The play’s always been something of an archival mystery and wonder as the play changed so much over the years, it’s taken years to pin down the various manuscripts of the different versions. All this for a play that Alan Ayckbourn eventually said of, “I should have left it alone!”

The complete guide to Alan Ayckbourn’s plays continues with one of his most famous works.

How The Other Half Loves premiered at Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre, Scarborough, on 31 July 1969 and was hugely popular.

It’s long been argued it was a revolutionary play in being the first to depict two spaces overlaid over each other with action happening simultaneously in both spaces and which - in one scene - also take place simultaneously on different days. It marked the true start of Alan Ayckbourn’s continuous experimentation with form and structure in his writing.

Sadly, these points were lost when it famously transferred to London in 1970 with an end-stage production starring Robert Morley, who no doubt made the play a huge success but changed it beyond recognition with his improvisations and constant unapproved alterations to the script. The ensemble and experimental nature of the piece was lost beneath the weight of his personality and fame!

On the plus side, the play was financially a huge success and it cemented Alan Ayckbourn as one of the West End’s hottest playwriting properties.

How The Other Half Loves has subsequently become one of Alan Ayckbourn’s most performed and popular works and has been revived in the West End on several occasions.

Original manuscripts for the play are held in the Ayckbourn Archive at the Borthwick Institute for Archives and at the British Library.

As we reach week 15 of the complete guide to Alan Ayckbourn’s plays, we reach his first West End transfer and a play which received such biting reviews that Alan almost decided to give up playwriting!

Mr Whatnot opened at the Victoria Theatre, Stoke-on-Trent, on 12 November 1963 and features a mute protagonist in a surreal work which is dependent on more than 300 sound cues (this being the early ‘60s in a regional theatre, that was quite a technical challenge!)

The play transferred to the New Arts Theatre, London, on 6 August 1964 and despite featuring Ronnie Barker in the cast, the play closed 16 days later having garnered some of the worse reviews of Alan’s entire career.

Dispirited, Alan vowed to give up playwriting and joined the BBC as a Radio Drama Producer for five years.

Mr Whatnot would go on to become a success though and Alan himself successfully revived it to open the Stephen Joseph Theatre in the Round in 1976. It has been performed around the world and is the earliest of Alan’s plays to be available to produce and which has also been published.

Original manuscripts are very rare with the British Library holding one of the few known original scripts.

Find out more at http://mrwhatnot.alanayckbourn.net or by clicking the link in the bio.

The complete guide to Alan Ayckbourn's plays (week 14) and we’re back to an obscurity!

Follow The Lover is a little-known one act play that was first presented - probably - in March 1962. We actually know so little about the play that it’s difficult to ascertain many hard facts about it.

It was probably only been performed once and it appears that performance was unlicensed (until 1968, all public performances had to be licensed by the Lord Chamberlain), which may explain why it was never performed again.

It was presented in an amateur production by Scarborough Theatre Guild at The Library Theatre, Scarborough, starring Alan and the Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre’s manager Ken Boden, directed by Ken’s wife, Margaret.

It follows a couple who each believe the other is having an affair. They each hire detectives to investigate, thus compounding the suspicions of each other.

The play was attributed to Alan’s early pseudonym, Roland, Allen, and only two copies of the play are known to exist in the British Library and the Ayckbourn Archive at the Borthwick Institute for Archives.

It has never been published and is unavailable to perform and is considered one of the playwright’s ‘Grey Plays’; produced once but never to be performed again.

Find out more at http://followthelover.alanayckbourn.net or clicking the link in the bio.

Week 10 of the complete guide to Alan Ayckbourn's plays & we’re now at the fourth play in the full-length canon.

Standing Room Only marks a significant step forward for the playwright. It was his first play to be optioned for the West End and for television - although neither were produced.

It is also his first work of ’speculative fiction’ being set in a grid-locked London in 2010 where a totalitarian government has stamped down on unauthorised pregnancies and is clandestinely sterilising much of the population.

It is also the first play to be attributed to Alan Ayckbourn rather than his pseudonym Roland Allen. Premiered on 13 July 1961 at Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre, Scarborough, it was attributed to Roland Allen. But when revived - and extensively revised - in 1962 by the author at the Victoria Theatre, Stone-on-Trent, it was attributed to Alan Ayckbourn. Every play subsequently has been attributed to Alan Ayckbourn.

Original manuscripts for Standing Room Only are held in the Borthwick Institute for Archives at the University of York.

Week 9 of the complete guide to Alan Ayckbourn's plays & we’re now at the third play in the full-length canon.

Dad’s Tale is Alan Ayckbourn’s first Christmas play, his first play for children and his only play which includes ballet sequences. It has also never been published, never performed again after its first production and has been withdrawn by the playwright for production practically since then.

The world premiere was at Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre on 19 December 1960 and was a complete flop as, aimed at schools and families, no-one appeared to have checked that schools had broken up by the time the show began! Audiences were… disappointing.

It was a co-production with the British Dance Drama Council and Alan had no idea this was the case until after he’d accepted the commission and was then told not to forget to put ballet into it!

The plot - as it is - sees a poor family stripped of all their possessions and Christmas Dinner by bailiffs on Christmas Day, who then dream of better times before the father is turned into a budgie… It’s fair to say, this is no classic.

Week 8 of the complete guide to Alan Ayckbourn's plays & it’s another obscure one.

After the success of his first two professional plays, The Square Cat and Love After All, in 1959, Alan Ayckbourn suddenly found favour with Scarborough’s amateur community which was keen for him to write them plays.

Double Hitch was written for Scarborough Theatre Guild and premiered circa 1960 - there’s some debate about this as the Lord Chamberlain’s Office has a license for performance for 1962, however we know it was publicly performed - without license - several times prior to that. Which was a tad naughty.

The play was performed at the Library Theatre as well as at St John’s Presbyterian Church and several drama festivals in the town in double or triple bills. It follows two couples who find themselves double-booked into the same creepy cottage and the misunderstandings and confusions which arise from that.

It’s considered the first of Alan Ayckbourn’s ‘Grey Plays’; these are plays which have had public performances but have subsequently been withdrawn, have never been published and are not available for production. They are not considered part of the official Ayckbourn play canon.

The only known complete original manuscript is held in the Lord Chamberlain’s Collection at the British Library.

Week 7 of the exhaustive & complete guide to Alan Ayckbourn's Plays & we're now at his second canonical full-length play.

Love After All was commissioned in the immediate aftermath of the success of The Square Cat and it was written at speed - between commission and first performance, there was just three months.

It premiered at the Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre, Scarborough, on 21 December 1959.

It was inspired by The Barber of Seville and is Alan's only fully period play, being set during Edwardian times. Although its initial success led to it being revived in 1960 when the director insisted it be rewritten to a contemporary setting.

The play is attributed to his pseudonym , Roland Allen, as Alan intended to star in the original production. National Service put paid to that, but he did appear in the 1960 revival.

It was never performed again and Alan tells the story he tried to destroy all copies of this play. It was believed lost until 2007 when his archivist, Simon Murgatroyd, worked with the British Library and found the only surviving copy of the original version of the play - no copy of the revised manuscript survives.

The sole surviving Love After All manuscript is held in the Lord Chamberlain's Collection at the British Library. It's never been published and is not available to perform.

Week 5 of The Ayckbourn Plays & we've finally got a play you might recognise!

The Square Cat is Alan Ayckbourn's first professionally produced play and opened at the Theatre in the Round at the Library Theatre, Scarborough, on 30 July 1959.

It was commissioned after Alan complained to the company's artistic director, Stephen Joseph, about the quality of the roles he was playing. Stephen challenged him, if you can do better, write a play and if it's any good I'll direct it - but you have to play the lead.

So Alan did, he wrote the play in early 1959 - with a little help from his wife, Christine Roland - and Stephen Joseph liked it and Alan played the role-swapping lead character of flamboyant rock & roll star Jerry Wattis and his mild-mannered alter-ego Arthur Brummage.

The play was a huge success in the 1959 summer season and swiftly led to Alan being commissioned for a second work. More importantly, it kickstarted Alan's playwriting career which is still going strong 60 years on.

Manuscripts of The Square Cat are held in the Ayckbourn Archive at the Borthwick Institute for Archives, in the Lord Chamberlain's Collection at the British Library and in the John Roland's Library at the University of Manchester.

Attributed to Alan's early writing pseudonym Roland Allen, it's never been published and is not available to perform, but is hugely significant for the playwright and his career.

Week 2 of The Ayckbourn Plays & it’s The Party Game. Written c.1958 & unknown until it’s discovery in a Scarborough loft in 2007.

Never performed, but a fascinating work, it centres on a party where the main guest - a theatre critic - never arrives. Full of witticisms & one of the bleakest endings in an Ayckbourn play, it was offered for amateur performance, but turned down written as it was by an unperformed & untested playwright.

The Party Game is held in the Ayckbourn Archive at the Borthwick Institute for Archives.

Find out more at http://the party game.alanayckbourn.net

Lady Edith’s Drive: Actually, this photograph was taken at a rather unfortunate moment as poor Edith has lost all sight of her drive under twelve feet of snow..
